meta.title: Who really said "Beatles Rejection: We Don't Like Their Sound. Groups of Guitars Are On Their Way Out"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Brian Epstein wrote it down — he never said it. The man he quoted was Decca’s Dick Rowe, in different words, and Rowe denied it for life.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beatles Rejection: We Don't Like Their Sound. Groups of Guitars Are On Their Way Out'?
meta.ogDescription: Epstein reported it; Decca’s Dick Rowe allegedly said it. The primary source reads “groups of four guitarists” — and Rowe always denied it.

answer.label: Not Brian Epstein — actually Decca’s Dick Rowe
answer.authorDates: 1921–1986 · British record producer, head of A&R (Singles) at Decca
answer.sourceLine: Brian Epstein is the source of this anecdote, not its author — in it, he is the man being turned down. Epstein’s 1964 memoir A Cellarful of Noise quotes Decca’s Dick Rowe telling him “Not to mince words, Mr. Epstein, we don’t like your boys’ sound. Groups of four guitarists are on the way out.” The tidier sentence people share today is a later compression, and Rowe rejected the whole attribution until he died in 1986.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Brian Epstein · Doubleday, Garden City, New York, 1964 (LCCN 64024896)
Chapter 5, “No!”, page 46 — the locator Quote Investigator gives, verified there against scans
Dick Rowe, head of A&R (Singles), Decca Records — who denied ever saying it

source.excerpt: We had coffee, and Mr. Rowe, a short plump man, said to me: “Not to mince words, Mr. Epstein, we don’t like your boys’ sound. Groups of four guitarists are on the way out.” I said, masking the cold disappointment which had spread over me: “You must be out of your mind. These boys are going to explode. I am completely confident that one day they will be bigger than Elvis Presley.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ names the earliest evidence as Brian Epstein’s A Cellarful of Noise (1964), chapter 5, page 46 — verified there against scans — where the words belong to Dick Rowe and read “Groups of four guitarists are on the way out.”

The same survey shows the compact modern wording entering print fifteen years later, in Stephen Pile’s The Book of Heroic Failures, first published in 1979 — page 215 of the 1981 Futura reprint Quote Investigator verified — credited to no person at all but to “Decca Recording Company”. Compare the versions ↗

Wikipedia’s entry for Dick Rowe ↗ (9 June 1921 – 6 June 1986) confirms he ran Decca’s singles A&R desk, that Epstein’s book is where the remark is pinned on him, and that he denied ever having said it.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the 1964 Doubleday first edition ↗ (Garden City, N.Y.; LCCN 64024896) matches the edition Quote Investigator scanned. Its scan is lending-restricted, so the page-46 locator here rests on Quote Investigator, not on our own reading.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the 1964 Doubleday edition, page 46. Note the wording: groups of four guitarists, not the “groups of guitars” that circulates now. The Internet Archive’s copy of that edition is lending-restricted, so we did not read the page ourselves.

author.name: Dick Rowe
author.heading: About Dick Rowe
author.metaLine: 1921–1986 · British record producer · head of A&R (Singles), Decca Records
author.bio: Richard Paul Brutton Rowe ran Decca’s singles A&R department from the 1950s to the 1970s and was known in the trade as “the man with the golden ear” — he discovered or signed the Rolling Stones, Van Morrison, Tom Jones, Cat Stevens, the Moody Blues, Procol Harum and the Animals. Popular music history remembers him for one decision instead: the Beatles auditioned for Decca on 1 January 1962 and were turned down in favour of Brian Poole and the Tremeloes. He spent the rest of his life denying he ever said the sentence that made him famous.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two separate things get muddled here: who said it, and what was actually said.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s own list of candidate speakers includes him, and it is his book the line lives in — but Epstein is the source of the story, not its author. His 1964 memoir is where the remark first appears, and in it he is the man on the receiving end. Quote Investigator traces the line to that book ↗

The crisp version entered circulation through Stephen Pile’s The Book of Heroic Failures (1979), which pins it on the company rather than a person; later quotation collections copied that framing. See the 1979 and 1998 citations ↗

items.who: “Groups of guitars are on the way out”
items.why: Epstein’s book has “Groups of four guitarists are on the way out”; Hunter Davies’s 1968 authorised biography renders it in reported speech. The direct quotation people share is a tightening of both. Compare the wordings ↗
Rowe is the man Epstein names, and he is the best answer available — but he is not a corroborating witness. He rejected the attribution for the rest of his life, as his biography records ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: Decca’s Dick Rowe told Brian Epstein his boys’ sound was not wanted and that “groups of four guitarists are on the way out” — as Epstein set it down two years later in A Cellarful of Noise ↗. Everything tidier than that is later polish.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Decca did not fumble the Beatles out of pure stupidity. On 1 January 1962 the band came down from Liverpool to Decca Studios in West Hampstead and cut fifteen songs — an unusually long test — and the label then had to choose between them and Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, who were based nearer London and would be easier to work with. Decca took the Tremeloes.

What makes the sentence immortal is not simply that it was wrong, but that it was so specifically, so quotably wrong, at the exact moment the guitar group was about to swallow popular music whole. That is also why it kept getting shorter: a line that good gets sanded smoother every time it is retold.
detailsBody: Epstein’s memoir appeared in 1964, by which point the Beatles were the biggest act on earth — which is to say the anecdote was first written down at the moment it was most enjoyable to tell, by the man it made look prescient. That does not make it false. It does mean the only witness account in existence is a two-year-old memory recorded by an interested party, and that the man it accuses spent the rest of his life contradicting it.

Rowe’s reputation survived rather better than the joke suggests. He went on to sign the Rolling Stones — on George Harrison’s recommendation — along with Van Morrison, Tom Jones, the Moody Blues and the Animals, which is why the trade called him the man with the golden ear rather than the man who turned down the Beatles.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest evidence is Epstein’s A Cellarful of Noise (1964), ch. 5, p. 46, quoting Dick Rowe: "Groups of four guitarists are on the way out."

The compact wording "We don’t like their sound. Groups of guitars are on the way out." first appears in Stephen Pile, The Book of Heroic Failures (1979), p. 215, credited to "Decca Recording Company".
Hunter Davies, The Beatles: The Authorized Biography (1968), p. 131, reports it in indirect speech.
Dick Rowe lived 9 June 1921 to 6 June 1986, was head of A&R (Singles) at Decca, and denied ever saying the line.
The Beatles auditioned at Decca Studios, West Hampstead, on 1 January 1962; Decca signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead, partly because they were based nearer London.
A Cellarful of Noise by Brian Epstein was published by Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., in 1964 (LCCN 64024896); the scan is lending-restricted.
